Case study · 03 / 04

Planty — rebranding an e-commerce subscription service for growth.

Role Product & Marketing Manager
Company Planty UK
Year 2022 — 2023
Focus UX / UI · Conversion · Brand
01 — Context

A small e-commerce subscription outgrowing its own website.

Planty is a UK-based subscription service delivering bespoke vegan food. I joined in 2021 and grew with the business — starting in marketing & operations, then product, and stepping into an interim CMO role for a year during a leadership gap.

By mid-2022 the brand was stretched thin. The site we'd launched with couldn't keep up: customers were bouncing off a subscription flow that asked too much too early; the visual identity no longer matched where the product had landed; and retention was leaking through avoidable friction.

The CEO and I co-led a full rebrand and website relaunch — my role spanned product direction, UX, content, and the commercial framing that tied it all together.

Jump to the results ↓
02 — Problem

The site didn't match the product — or the people buying it.

Three issues kept surfacing across every input we had — customer feedback, behaviour data and team conversations:

Where the signal came from
  1. User interviews with current and lapsed subscribers
  2. Customer surveys sent across the active base
  3. Competitor analysis across vegan and meal-kit categories
  4. Recurring themes from customer service queries

Triangulating those four inputs, three issues rose to the top — and shaped the rest of the project:

Issue 01

An overloaded, dated site.

Across the whole site — not just the homepage — visitors had to parse too much before they could grasp what Planty actually was, and what set it apart from any other vegan box.

Issue 02

Restricted + confusing subscription controls.

The off-the-shelf tool gave customers almost no way to manage their own subscription — no option to skip or pause a delivery, and no reminders or direction to guide them. The gaps bred confusion, and people cancelled outright rather than work around them.

Issue 03

Brand identity behind the product.

The visual system hadn't evolved alongside new product ranges and partnerships. It looked like an early-stage startup; the offering had grown past that.

03 — Approach

A rebrand and a bespoke build, run as one project.

The CEO and I ran the brand and the product work in parallel, both of us hands-on across UX and UI. Every visual decision carried a UX consequence and vice versa, so we designed them together — user journeys, content, the bespoke website and subscription flow, and the visual identity itself.

Because the team was small, the process was deliberately compact: weekly working sessions, a prioritised backlog in Notion, and a shared principle we kept coming back to — make the right action the easiest action.

04 — Key moves

Where the product changed most.

Three moves did the heaviest lifting — the new subscription system, a full rebrand, and a smarter set of email flows. Each one, with the work behind it:

Move 01

A custom subscription system

We moved off the off-the-shelf tool and built our own: one-tap skip and pause, a cancellation-reason questionnaire, order-reminder notification banners, clearer status tags, and a cleaner account UX throughout — surfaced in email, on the homepage for logged-in users, and from the dashboard. Direct effect on churn.

The subscription systemBuilt in-house · 2023

Move 02

A rebrand across the whole brand

Not just the website — a new visual identity carried end to end, from a simpler homepage and sign-up flow to meal packaging, print and out-of-home. One consistent system: bold Ostrich Sans headlines, top-down food photography, and the new Planty lockup.

The comms system & applicationsBRAND IDENTITY · 2022

The websiteRelaunch · 2023

Move 03

Email flows that add up

I analysed customer behaviour and the data behind it — churn, drop-off points, where people went quiet — and used that to redesign the whole email flow from the ground up. Instead of a one-size-fits-all newsletter, customers now get genuinely useful, well-timed messages: order reminders, cancellation confirmations, re-activation emails, and lifecycle nudges mapped to specific moments — first box, mid-subscription, at-risk, win-back — each reinforcing the same actions the new account made easy.

05 — Outcome

A product that finally felt like itself.

After launch, the numbers moved — retention up 30%, acquisition doubled, partnership channels growing 52%. But the more telling signal came from customer service: the volume of subscription-related complaints dropped dramatically, because people could now do the thing they wanted to do without contacting us.

What I take from this project: rebrands are product decisions. The moment you change how something looks, you also change what it feels like to use — and if the product experience hasn't caught up, the new visual layer just makes the friction more visible.

+30% Retention uplift

After launching the custom subscription system and optimised email flows.

2× Acquisition doubled

Clearer site + improved sign-up flow post-relaunch.

+52% Partnership channel growth

Product launches & strategic industry partnerships together.

The rebrand only worked because the UX was fixed alongside it.

Launching new visuals on top of the old friction would have been louder, not better. Every brand decision had to earn its place in the user's flow.
